entries.title: Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams
entries.summary: This post presents a five-stage operating model for managing Amazon Bedrock cost: attribute every dollar to an owner, make every request observable, enforce budgets, optimize platform defaults, and operate a review cadence. Written for FinOps and platform engineering teams.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams

Cost management for generative AI is a shared responsibility between the teams that build applications and the teams accountable for cloud spend. Many teams start by comparing per-model token rates and asking application teams to shorten prompts. Those steps help, but they don’t answer the questions that finance and engineering leaders ask as usage scales: which team spent this, on which workload, and was that spend inside an approved budget?

Agentic workloads make those questions more pressing. A conversational assistant typically issues one model invocation per user turn. An agentic workflow, such as an AI coding assistant that plans a change, reads files, calls tools, and iterates, issues many invocations per task and carries a larger context on each one. Token consumption therefore scales with the degree of autonomy you grant the workflow and the size of the context it carries, rather than with the number of user interactions. Because consumption is a function of how a workload is designed and operated, cost management for generative AI is an architectural and operational discipline. Published averages are a poor substitute for your own numbers: use the AWS Pricing Calculator and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page to model rates, and use Step 2 of this post to measure what your workloads actually consume.

The fix isn’t a cheaper model or a smaller prompt. It’s an operating model: a repeatable loop that attributes every dollar to an owner, makes every request observable, alerts on and enforces budgets before overspend compounds, optimizes the platform defaults that drive most waste, and reviews the whole system on a cadence.

In this post, you learn how to manage Amazon Bedrock cost in five steps. You attribute every dollar to an owner, make every request observable, control spend with budgets and enforcement, optimize the platform defaults that drive most avoidable spend, and operate a review cadence that turns data into decisions. This approach is built from AWS building blocks, and you can customize it and apply it to your own environment. The post is written for two audiences: FinOps practitioners who own attribution, chargeback, budgets, and anomaly review, and platform engineering teams who own logging, request metadata, enforcement, and routing defaults.

The operating model in one view

Five stages, run as a loop. Attribute: every Amazon Bedrock dollar lands on an identity, team, and application in the billing pipeline. Observe: every request is logged with enough metadata to explain what generated the spend. Enforce: budgets have teeth, with alerts at minimum and hard blocks where the risk demands them. Optimize: the platform defaults (model routing, caching, token limits) remove waste centrally instead of asking every team to be careful. Operate: a small scorecard and a review cadence turn the data into decisions. FinOps leads stages one and five. Platform engineering leads two through four. The review is joint. The stages are sequenced deliberately. Each one depends on the ones before it, and teams that jump straight to optimization without attribution and observability are guessing.

Stage 1: Attribute every dollar

You can’t manage what you can’t attribute, and everything downstream (chargeback, budgets, enforcement, anomaly detection) depends on this stage. The foundation is the granular cost attribution of Amazon Bedrock (see Introducing granular cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock): Amazon Bedrock automatically attributes inference costs to the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal that made the call, across all models, with no resources to manage. The caller’s ARN lands in the 

line_item_iam_principal
column of the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0, and coverage spans IAM users, roles, federated identities, and API keys.

Setup is four steps:

  • Turn on IAM principal data in your CUR 2.0 data export.
  • Tag your IAM principals with business dimensions such as team, application, and cost center. For federated access, configure your identity provider to pass session names and tags through OIDC or SAML claims.
  • Activate those tags as cost allocation tags in AWS Billing (console or the 
    UpdateCostAllocationTagsStatus
    API).
  • Analyze the tags: they surface in CUR 2.0 with an 
    iamPrincipal/
    prefix (for example, 
    iamPrincipal/team
    ) and appear in AWS Cost Explorer under the IAM category within 24–48 hours of activation, ready for filtering and grouping by team, application, or cost center.

This is invoice-grade, per-identity attribution with no custom infrastructure.

The shared-role problem

The pattern that deserves the most attention is the shared-role problem, because it is where most platforms silently lose attribution. A large language model (LLM) gateway that calls Amazon Bedrock through a single IAM role attributes every dollar to that one role, eliminating per-user visibility entirely. The fix is per-user session management. The gateway assumes the Amazon Bedrock invocation role once per user, passing the user’s identity as the role session name and their attributes as session tags, then caches those credentials for up to an hour (one AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) call per user per hour, not per request).

This needs two roles: a gateway execution role holding 

sts:AssumeRole
and 
sts:TagSession
permissions, and the Amazon Bedrock invocation role it assumes. The result is 
line_item_iam_principal
entries like 
assumed-role/BedrockRuntimeRole/gw-alex
, each carrying its user’s tags: per-user and per-tenant attribution restored behind a shared gateway.

A note on application inference profiles and Projects

Amazon Bedrock offers two more attribution mechanisms, each suited to a different pattern. Application inference profiles are pre-created, per-application resources on the 

bedrock-runtime
endpoint that carry cost allocation tags. You create one profile per application per model per AWS Region, and callers reference the profile ARN, which fits teams with a small and stable set of applications and models. Projects and workspaces serve the 
bedrock-mantle
endpoint (Responses API, Chat Completions API). A project isn’t tied to a specific model, so a single project ID spans many models, which fits teams whose model usage changes frequently. You pass the project ID at client initialization, and its tags flow to CUR 2.0 and Cost Explorer (see Manage AI costs with Amazon Bedrock Projects). Projects are the attribution path for OpenAI-compatible workloads on Amazon Bedrock.

For 

bedrock-runtime
workloads, we recommend IAM principal attribution through session tags as the primary mechanism. It scales with your identity system, requires no pre-created resources, and covers every model and API operation. Application inference profiles work well when a small, stable set of business units needs invoice-grade billing separation without changes to identity design. Use projects for 
bedrock-mantle
workloads that use the Responses API or Chat Completions API.

Stage 2: Make every request observable

CUR tells you who spent. Invocation logs tell you what happened. Amazon Bedrock supports model invocation logging of request data, response data, and metadata to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), or both. Use Amazon CloudWatch for fast operational queries and S3 plus Amazon Athena for long-term business intelligence (BI) access. Treat logging as infrastructure, not a manual toggle: provision the log group or bucket through code, define retention and encryption policies, and validate delivery during environment setup. If logging exists only in development or only in one Region, your cost program becomes fragmentary the moment usage grows.

Logging also closes the latency gap: CUR attribution lags roughly 24 hours, but CloudWatch plus OpenTelemetry can power near-real-time dashboards showing per-developer spend within minutes (Analyzing Claude Code usage with CloudWatch and OpenTelemetry demonstrates this end to end).

Request metadata for workload-level attribution

Raw logs answer identity-level questions. To answer workload-level questions (which feature, workflow, or tenant generated the tokens), stamp request metadata on every call. Amazon Bedrock captures this metadata in the invocation logs for later analysis:

The following example uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock through the US cross-Region inference profile. For the full list of models, see Supported foundation models in Amazon Bedrock. For availability by Region, see Model support by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

Amazon Bedrock doesn’t enforce request metadata, and teams drift into inconsistent schemas quickly when every application does its own thing. The platform team should inject mandatory metadata centrally in a shared SDK wrapper or gateway, normalize the key set, and treat metadata coverage as a platform health metric.

Diagnostic queries

With logs and metadata in place, CloudWatch Logs Insights answers the standing questions. Who consumes the most tokens:

The same query grouped by 

requestMetadata.application
and 
requestMetadata.workflow
instead of 
caller
produces the workload-level leaderboard: the view product and engineering teams will ask FinOps for the moment chargeback conversations start.

Note: Field paths shown in the preceding query are illustrative. Verify against your invocation log schema, which may vary by model, API operation, and logging configuration.

Stage 3: Enforce budgets

With attribution and observability in place, enforcement becomes an architecture choice rather than a wish. There are three viable tiers. The right one depends on your spend velocity, your risk tolerance for overspend, and how your tools connect to Amazon Bedrock.

Tier 1: Monitor and alert (no blocking)

Amazon Bedrock writes principal identity into the billing pipeline automatically. You put AWS Budgets on top for threshold alerts, with the OpenTelemetry dashboards from Stage 2 closing the 24-hour CUR gap for day-to-day visibility. Nothing to deploy, native AWS billing, and no added latency on inference calls. It works with tools that call Amazon Bedrock directly. Nothing can hard-stop spend, so you see the problem after it happens. Right for early adoption, where alerting plus human intervention is sufficient. Two builder guides walk through it: Limiting Bedrock usage and controlling costs, and Deep dive on managing Bedrock in Claude Code with AWS Budgets and Tags.

Tier 2: IAM tag enforcement (deny on breach)

An aggregator AWS Lambda function tallies per-user token and dollar counters in Amazon DynamoDB from invocation log data. When a user breaches their threshold, the function adds their identity to a shared IAM deny policy (denying 

bedrock:*
) until a monthly reset or admin override. This enforcement runs entirely on IAM and Amazon Bedrock logging, with no third-party component in the inference path, and it works with tools that call Amazon Bedrock directly. The Guidance for Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock in the AWS Solutions Library provides a deployable variant. It checks each user’s usage against per-user and per-team limits when it issues credentials, and withholds credentials once a user exceeds their limit. Because that check uses usage telemetry emitted by the client, its figures can differ from CUR. In either form, enforcement is asynchronous. A block takes effect seconds to minutes after the breaching call for an IAM policy update, or at the next credential refresh for the credential check. Your platform team owns the pipeline. This tier is right for teams that need real enforcement, can tolerate that lag, and want to keep third-party software out of the data path.

Tier 3: Gateway enforcement (synchronous block)

A gateway sits in the inference data path and enforces budgets synchronously, returning HTTP 429 the moment a user or team exceeds their limit. You get sub-second blocking, per-user model allowlists, token rate limits, and centrally enforced routing rules. The trade-off: a component in the data path that must be deployed, scaled, and security-reviewed. Clients must be configured to send their requests through the gateway.

For Claude Code and Claude Desktop fleets, the Claude apps gateway for AWS is the official recommendation. It ships inside the CLI binary and runs as a single stateless container backed by PostgreSQL. It provides OIDC identity, centrally managed policy, OpenTelemetry telemetry, multi-Region Amazon Bedrock routing, and per-user/group/org spend caps out of the box. For mixed-model workloads spanning multiple providers, general-purpose gateways remain the right choice: LiteLLM through the Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate reference architecture, or a serverless alternative described in Build a proactive AI cost management system for Amazon Bedrock, Part 2.

Choosing a tier

Two factors dominate.

Connectivity: If developers call Amazon Bedrock directly with no proxy, only Tiers 1 and 2 are viable.

Spend velocity: If spend is already in the millions per month, build enforcement now. If alerts can hold the line for another quarter, invest in Stages 1 and 2 first and add enforcement when the data demands it.

Most organizations should phase it: observe at Tier 1, then step up. Treat all three as bridges, not destinations: the Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens already codifies agent cost governance as a first-class architectural concern, and the attribution foundation from Stage 1 is what any managed enforcement will sit on.

Stage 4: Optimize the defaults

Most Amazon Bedrock waste is not individual carelessness. It is platform defaults nobody set. The two highest-impact levers are both platform-controlled.

Model routing

Not every task needs a frontier model. Routine completions (boilerplate, linting suggestions, small refactors) can run on smaller, cheaper models with quality reserved for complex reasoning, through intelligent prompt routing within a model family or routing rules at the gateway (see Reduce costs and latency with Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing and prompt caching for the full walkthrough). Which workflows can downshift is an empirical question: pull the workload leaderboard from Stage 2, run a quality evaluation on the cheaper model for the top entries, and route what passes. For agentic coding fleets, where boilerplate dominates call volume, more than half of calls landing on cheaper models is an achievable target.

Prompt caching

Prompt caching rewards stable repeated prefixes. As of October 2026, the published Amazon Bedrock pricing for Anthropic Claude models in US East (N. Virginia) bills a cache write at 1.25x the base input rate with the 5-minute time-to-live (TTL) (2x with the 1-hour TTL). A cache read is billed at 0.1x the base input rate on Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Haiku 4.5, and at 0.05x on Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5. Check the pricing page for your model and Region, because these multipliers vary by model and can change. The break-even math is friendlier than teams assume. With the 5-minute TTL, a single reuse already pays for the write, and ten calls against a stable prefix cost roughly a fifth of the uncached price (about 22 percent at a 0.1x read rate, 17 percent at 0.05x). The only losing case is writes that are never re-read, which cost 25 percent extra with the 5-minute TTL and double with the 1-hour TTL. So the platform dashboard should track cache-read volume against cache-write volume per workflow. A low read ratio means the prefix is not actually stable (usually a timestamp or session ID embedded before the cache point).

Candidates surface directly from the invocation logs:

Note: Field paths shown in the preceding query are illustrative. Verify against your invocation log schema, which may vary by model, API operation, and logging configuration.

Application-level optimization

A third class of savings (just-in-time retrieval instead of stuffed context, compaction of long conversations, distilling stable high-volume workflows onto smaller models) belongs to application teams rather than the platform. The platform’s job is to make those savings visible: publish the per-workflow token leaderboard, set token limits per model and workflow, and let the teams that own expensive workflows see exactly where they stand.

Stage 5: Operate the loop

The first four stages produce data. This one turns it into decisions. The platform team runs a standing health dashboard with four signals:

  • Model mix: Which models are called and how often, the direct measure of routing discipline.
  • Failed request rates: Errors, throttles, and timeouts. Each retry adds latency, and a client-side timeout on a request that still completes on the service side can be billed twice, once for the abandoned call and once for the retry.
  • Cache effectiveness: The read-versus-write ratio from Stage 4.
  • Metadata coverage: The percentage of production calls with complete metadata. Every uncovered call is an attribution blind spot that quietly degrades every other number.

When a signal drifts, the remediation is a policy change (routing rules, token limits, metadata enforcement), not an email asking teams to be careful.

The money loop

FinOps runs the money loop on the same data. When attribution is clean, anomaly detection becomes an investigation stream rather than a panicked all-hands: a spike in a tagged team or application triggers a lookup in the Stage 2 leaderboard, not a war room. Chargeback runs from CUR groupings by team and application.

Scorecard

The following thresholds are starting points, not prescriptions. Calibrate them against your own fleet data and pricing tier before adopting them as policy.

DimensionMetricGreenYellowRed
Unit economicsCost per successful outcome≤ budget1–1.5x budget>1.5x budget
Per-dev costDaily spend per developer<$100$100–$300>$300
Model routing% of calls to cost-efficient-models>50%30–50%<30%
Cache efficiencyCache-read hit ratio>60%30–60%<30%

Green means the workload operates inside its economic envelope. Yellow means routing or caching discipline is slipping. Red means spend is concentrating in premium models or uncached context, and the Stage 3 and 4 controls are the remediation path. Review this scorecard on a regular cadence (weekly for high-velocity fleets, biweekly otherwise) and treat it as the joint FinOps-plus-platform decision surface.

Conclusion

In this post, you learned how to build a five-stage operating model that takes Amazon Bedrock spend from uncontrolled to fully governed:

  • Attribute every dollar to an owner using IAM principal tags, session tags, and CUR 2.0.
  • Observe every request through model invocation logging and stamped request metadata.
  • Enforce budgets at the tier that matches your risk: monitor-only, IAM deny on breach, or synchronous gateway blocking.
  • Optimize platform defaults with intelligent prompt routing and prompt caching to remove waste centrally.
  • Operate a scorecard and review cadence that turns telemetry into policy decisions.

Notice the first row of that scorecard: cost per successful outcome, not cost per call. That distinction is where this playbook hands off. Everything here makes Amazon Bedrock spend visible, attributable, capped, and efficient, but a workflow can be perfectly efficient and still not be worth running. Deciding that requires measuring the agent against the human process it replaced, which is a product and analytics discipline rather than a FinOps one. What the cost platform contributes is the foundation: clean attribution and per-workflow cost data are exactly the inputs that outcome measurement joins against.

Build the five stages and you can answer, end to end: who spent it, why, and whether it was controlled. That is what it means to manage Amazon Bedrock cost, and it is the difference between a monthly bill review and an operating model.

To get started, deploy the Guidance for Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock reference architecture for Stages 1–3, then use the cost attribution best practices documentation to configure your tagging strategy.

entries.title: Preview web apps live as your coding agent builds them with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
entries.summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Session endpoints give each runtime session an authenticated URL that forwards any HTTP method, path, and WebSocket connection to the ports you allow. In this post, you deploy a coding agent that keeps a Vite website running in its session, then watch the live site update in your browser as the agent edits files.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Preview web apps live as your coding agent builds them with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime

Coding agents now build working web apps: a dashboard, a product page, a prototype that a product team wants to try. The fastest way to review that work is to open the app, use it, ask for a change, and check the result. That loop works well when the app keeps running where the agent edits it, so each change shows up in the browser within seconds. When the app must be copied out and deployed somewhere else first, every change waits for a deployment, and the review slows down to that pace.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with your choice of agent framework and foundation model (FM). AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, runs each agent session in its own isolated microVM. With Session endpoints, you can open an app running in that session from your own browser. Session Endpoints give each session an authenticated URL that forwards each request’s HTTP method, path, query string, and body, and WebSocket connections, to the ports you allow. You can watch the page update as the agent saves each file.

In this post, you deploy a coding agent that keeps a Vite website running in its session, then open one local page with a chat on the left and the live website on the right. You ask the agent to switch the site to a dark color theme, follow its steps as they stream in, and watch the website change without a refresh. Finally, you look at what happens internally: a second port in the same session, and the requests the Session endpoint refuses.

The complete sample, including the notebook this post follows, is in the 14-remote-access folder of the agentcore-samples GitHub repo.

How Session endpoints work

Each session gets its own Session endpoint, and six details shape how you use it.

You choose which ports it reaches. You set 

allowedPorts
when you call CreateAgentRuntime: 1–5 entries, each a single port or a range within 8000–12000, excluding the reserved platform ports. Allowing a port doesn’t start a server, so your application must listen on it, bound to 
0.0.0.0
.

The URL arrives with the session. The InvokeAgentRuntime response carries it in the 

X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Session-Endpoint-Url
header, which SDKs that model it expose as 
sessionEndpointUrl
.

Every request is authenticated. For a runtime that uses AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), each HTTP request, HTTP/2 stream, and WebSocket handshake carries a Signature Version 4 (SigV4) signature. The caller also needs 

bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy
on the runtime and its runtime endpoint. For a runtime with an inbound JSON Web Token (JWT) authorizer, each request carries a bearer token instead. Knowing the URL doesn’t grant access.

The host name selects the port. Your client connects on port 443 regardless of the target port, and a prefix on the host name chooses the port inside the session:

It carries the protocols your server speaks. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 requests, including server-sent events and gRPC, and WebSocket connections all pass through. This walkthrough uses HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket.

It’s scoped to one session. The URL needs credentials on every request and lasts only as long as the session, so use it to build, test, and review what your agent produces. To serve an app to your users, deploy it to a hosting service such as AWS Amplify Hosting.

A browser can’t add a SigV4 signature or a bearer token to the requests a page makes on its own, so the Session endpoint client in the bedrock-agentcore SDK can open a local endpoint on your machine. Your browser opens 

http://localhost:8088
, and the local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and WebSocket handshake before forwarding it.

A Session endpoint is different from a runtime endpoint, which AgentCore runtime already provides. Use a runtime endpoint, such as 

DEFAULT
, to reach your agent, which controls which version of it callers will reach. 
InvokeAgentRuntime
calls resolve through it, so you can keep development and production on different versions and promote or roll back without changing callers. Use a Session endpoint to see what your agent runs in its session, such as a web preview. It’s an authenticated URL that reaches only the ports you allow, works with whichever version the session runs, and stops working when the session ends. For complete documentation, refer to Connect to runtime sessions through a session endpoint.

Solution overview

The sample has four parts. A coding agent runs in the session on port 8080 and edits the website’s files with four tools: list, read, write, and edit. The agent starts a Vite development server on port 8090, which serves the website and pushes each saved change to the browser over its hot-reload WebSocket. On your machine, 

PreviewApp
serves the preview page, sends your prompts to 
InvokeAgentRuntime
, and opens a local endpoint for the website. As Figure 1 shows, the preview page loads the website from the Vite development server on port 8090 through the local endpoint and the Session endpoint, and sends your prompts through 
InvokeAgentRuntime
to the agent on port 8080. The numbers show the order of the steps for one request.

Before step 1, 

PreviewApp
has already called 
InvokeAgentRuntime
once to start the session, which starts the agent and the Vite development server. 
PreviewApp
read the Session endpoint URL from that response and opened a local endpoint for port 8090. The numbered steps in Figure 1 then follow one request for a change:
  • The site pane of the preview page loads the website from the local endpoint on 
    localhost:8088
    . The local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and the WebSocket handshake, and forwards them to the Session endpoint. The Session endpoint checks the signature and the port against 
    allowedPorts
    , then forwards them to the Vite development server on port 8090. The page keeps the Vite hot-reload WebSocket open.
  • You send a prompt from the chat pane. 
    PreviewApp
    sends it to 
    InvokeAgentRuntime
    as a standard AWS API call signed with your AWS credentials, and the runtime delivers it to the agent on port 8080. The agent’s steps stream back to the chat pane as it works.
  • The agent calls Claude Haiku 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock to decide what to change.
  • The agent reads the site’s files and saves the ones it changes. The Vite development server serves those files and watches them for changes.
  • When a file is saved, Vite pushes the change over the WebSocket opened in step 1, back through the Session endpoint and the local endpoint, and the site pane updates without a refresh.
  • From the notebook, 
    PreviewApp
    reads the agent’s 
    /status
    route on port 8081 through the same Session endpoint. Only the port changes.

Port 8080 isn’t in 

allowedPorts
, because 
InvokeAgentRuntime
reaches the agent without going through the Session endpoint.

Prerequisites

To follow the walkthrough, you need:

  • An AWS account in an AWS Region where AgentCore runtime Session endpoints are available, with credentials configured.
  • Permissions to create an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, upload to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and create a runtime, plus 
    bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime
    and 
    bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy
    on that runtime and its 
    DEFAULT
    runtime endpoint. For details, refer to IAM permissions for AgentCore runtime.
  • Python 3.10 or later, with 
    bedrock-agentcore
    1.25.2 or later and 
    boto3
    1.43.122 or later.
  • Git, to clone the sample repo, and a Jupyter environment, such as JupyterLab or Visual Studio Code with the Jupyter extension, to run the notebook.
  • Access to Claude Haiku 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock. For model availability by Region, refer to Regional availability by models.
  • Node.js 22 or later with 
    npm
    , which the deployment script uses to package the agent and the website.

The sample deploys the agent as a zip file in Amazon S3 with direct code deployment for Node.js, so you don’t need Docker or an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository. Session endpoints work with microVM runtimes, not with the Instances compute type, and Session endpoint URLs are reachable over public HTTPS. AWS PrivateLink isn’t supported for inbound connections.

Deploy the agent and its website

First, you deploy the runtime, and the configuration you choose here decides which ports the Session endpoint can reach. The deployment script bundles the agent into one file, adds the website and its dependencies for the runtime’s Linux on Arm64 system, uploads the zip to Amazon S3, and creates the runtime.

The following excerpt from 

deploy.py
shows the two settings that matter for this post. 
protocolConfiguration
says where the agent listens for 
InvokeAgentRuntime
, and 
allowedPorts
lists the ports the Session endpoint can reach: 8090 for the website and 8081 for the agent’s status route. Port 8080 isn’t in the list, because 
InvokeAgentRuntime
reaches the agent without it. For the port and path settings, refer to Configure your agent’s serving port and invocation path.

The website’s Vite configuration makes the development server reachable from the Session endpoint. It listens on 

0.0.0.0
at port 8090 and doesn’t restrict the 
Host
header (
server.allowedHosts
is true), because requests arrive under a host name the runtime assigns rather than 
localhost
. The Session endpoint authenticates every request before it reaches the server, so the server doesn’t need its own host check.

To deploy the runtime:

1. Clone the sample repo and change to the sample folder:

2. Open 

session_endpoints_preview.ipynb
from the sample folder.

3. Run the install cell, which installs the Python dependencies.

4. Run the %run 

deploy.py
cell. Deployment takes a few minutes, mostly waiting for the runtime to reach the 
READY
status.

Open the preview

With the runtime ready, you start the preview. One call does three things: it starts a session (which starts the website), opens a local endpoint for port 8090, and serves the preview page on 

localhost:8087
.

Inside 

start()
, the calls that use Session endpoints are short. The first 
InvokeAgentRuntime
call returns the URL in a response header, 
session_endpoint_url
reads it, and the Session endpoint client opens a local endpoint for port 8090:

To open the preview:

  • Run the cell that starts 
    PreviewApp
    .
  • Open the printed link, 
    http://localhost:8087
    , in your browser.

The page shows the website on the right, served from port 8090 in the session, and a short guide with suggested requests on the left.

Ask the agent for a change

Now you ask for a change and watch it arrive. Each prompt goes to the agent through 

InvokeAgentRuntime
. The agent reads the files it needs, writes the ones it changes, and reports each step as it happens. When a file is saved, the Vite development server pushes the change over its WebSocket, through the Session endpoint and the local endpoint, and the website updates in place.

To ask for a change:

  • On the preview page, choose Switch this website to a dark coffee-house color theme.
  • Follow the agent’s steps in the chat pane as it reads and saves files.
  • Watch the site pane. It changes when the agent saves the stylesheet, and a banner names the file the change came from.

The following video shows the preview page while the agent works through several requests. Choosing a suggested request sends it to the agent, the chat pane lists each file the agent reads and saves, and the site pane on the right updates without a refresh, from the dark theme to a green Order ahead button.

The steps stream because the agent answers with server-sent events when you ask it to. You can send the same prompts from Python with 

app.ask
, which reads the stream with 
iter_events
from the 
bedrock-agentcore
SDK. The open page updates in the same way:

The output of this Python script should resemble the following:

Reach a second port in the same session

The website isn’t the only server you can reach. The agent serves 

/status
on port 8081, which lists each prompt and the files it changed. The same Session endpoint reaches it, and the only difference is the port argument.

The output of this Python script should resemble the following:

What the Session endpoint refuses

When the runtime refuses a request, it answers with an HTTP status, an empty body, and an error code in a response header, so you can tell its refusals from errors your application returns. The notebook sends a request to a port outside allowedPorts and a request without credentials, and the runtime refuses both with 403 AccessDenied.

The following table lists the refusals you’re likely to meet while you build with Session endpoints.

RequestResponse from the runtime
A port that isn’t in 
allowedPorts
 
403 AccessDenied
A request without valid credentials
403 AccessDenied
or 
401 AuthenticationRequired
An allowed port with nothing listening on it
502 PortNotReachable
A URL whose session no longer exists
404 SessionNotFound

How access to your session is protected

The runtime removes its own authentication headers before it forwards a request, so the website doesn’t receive your signature. Requests are recorded in AWS CloudTrail as 

InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy
events, with the event source 
bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com
. The local endpoint acts with your credentials, so it limits who can use it. It listens on 
127.0.0.1
only, answers only requests addressed to its own local address, and refuses WebSocket connections opened by pages from other origins. Run the local endpoint only while you use the preview. For more information, see Log session endpoint requests in CloudTrail.

The access controls don’t separate the website from the agent. Both run in the same session, so give the execution role only the permissions the agent needs. If the runtime replaces the session’s compute, open connections close, and the agent’s edits might not survive unless the session uses persistent storage. Refer to File system configurations for AgentCore runtime if you need the files to outlast the compute.

The agent’s file tools resolve every path inside the site folder and refuse paths outside it, so a prompt can’t make the agent change other files in the session. If other people can send prompts to your coding agent, consider Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter harmful prompts and responses, and review the agent’s changes before you publish them.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, stop the preview and delete the resources the sample created. The website the agent edited lives in the session, so it goes with the session.

To clean up:

1. Run the stop cell, and press Enter when the notebook asks. This stops the preview page, the local endpoint, and the session.

2. Run the %run 

cleanup.py
cell, which deletes the runtime, the uploaded code, and the IAM role.

Conclusion

Session endpoints give you authenticated access to the applications in an AgentCore runtime session from your own tools over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and WebSocket, on the ports you allow. In this post, you deployed a coding agent with a Vite website in its session, opened the live website in your browser through a local endpoint, asked the agent for a dark theme, and watched the change arrive as the agent saved the file. You also reached a second port in the same session and confirmed what the Session endpoint refuses.

To go further, run the notebook with your own site in the site folder, or change the agent’s tools to match how your coding agent works. For the full set of options, including port ranges, OAuth, HTTP/2, and gRPC, refer to Connect to runtime sessions through a session endpoint.

To change the port or path that 

InvokeAgentRuntime
uses in your own agent, refer to Configure your agent’s serving port and invocation path. If your agent also needs to run build or test commands in the same session, refer to Execute shell commands in AgentCore runtime sessions. To deploy your own Node.js agent from a zip file the way this sample does, refer to Direct code deployment for Node.js. For everything else the service offers, start with Host agent or tools with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, and find more examples in the agentcore-samples GitHub repo.

entries.title: How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock
entries.summary: Worldwide Express automated its less-than-truckload freight billing-exception process with a multi-agent solution built on Amazon Bedrock. Six months after launch, the company cut active exceptions by 75%, improved time-to-cash by four weeks, and unlocked $10 million in free cash flow.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock

Worldwide Express (part of ShipStation Global) had built something big: approximately $5 billion in systemwide revenue, over 75 less-than-truckload (LTL) carriers and more than 130,000 customers. But that same scale had a hidden cost. Every month, $15 million in free cash flow sat frozen, locked in billing exceptions no one had resolved yet. Each one had to be chased down by hand, carrier by carrier, with its own rules to check. Worldwide Express outsourced to a team that worked cases one at a time, calling customers and carriers for each dispute. The exceptions piled up, cash stayed stuck, and every order took longer to turn into money.

Worldwide Express worked with AWS and LTM to build a multi-agentic AI solution with Amazon Bedrock that plugs directly into their transportation management system (TMS), SpeedShip. Six months after launch, the company reported a 75 percent reduction in active exceptions, a 4-week improvement in time-to-cash, $1M annual savings, and a one-time $10M free cash flow infusion.

In this post, we describe the challenge, explain how Worldwide Express designed the multi-agent solution, and share the results.

The challenge

In LTL freight, roughly 14 percent of invoices fail the standard three-way match between the purchase order, the goods receipt, and the carrier invoice. When a match fails, the invoice enters exception handling. For Worldwide Express, exceptions fell into three categories:

  • Line-item mismatches: Quantities or service codes that didn’t align with the shipment record.
  • Pricing variances: The carrier billed a rate different from the contracted price.
  • Unexpected accessorial charges: Liftgate fees, residential surcharges, or reweigh adjustments that weren’t on the original quote.

Each exception triggered a five-step manual process:

  • Identify the exception type by cross-referencing the invoice against the purchase order, goods receipt, and pricing.
  • Research the root cause in vendor records.
  • Send email to the carrier or warehouse with dispute details.
  • Wait for a response.
  • Execute the resolution in the TMS.

With each carrier operating under its own tariff structure and dispute workflow, this process consumed most of the FinOps team’s bandwidth.

Rule-based process automation (RPA) can handle structured, predictable workflows. However, exception resolution requires contextual judgment: interpreting a carrier’s accessorial policy, comparing charges against shipment data, and deciding validity given a carrier, exception type, and dollar amount. That variability is what made the problem a fit for the agentic AI framework.

From assessment to production

In June 2025, Worldwide Express engaged the AWS Business Transformation & Value Advisory team to identify 19 automation opportunities across the Order-to-Cash lifecycle. Knowing the business value of exceptions automation, Worldwide Express moved from assessment to production in less than 6 months.

How it works

The solution runs on AWS. Amazon Bedrock provides AI reasoning, and Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is the engine. The design calls for fine-grained control over how each agent reasons, where decision boundaries sit, and how exceptions are routed between agents. Building the framework directly on Amazon EC2, with Amazon Bedrock providing inference, keeps that orchestration logic fully in the team’s hands and supports open source agent libraries. Production controls of business logic make each agent’s role, inputs, and decision boundaries explicit and auditable. In a billing-dispute workflow, every automated decision needs to be explainable.

Agents

When an invoice exception is detected, the system routes it to one of three specialized AI agents, each handling a specific type of billing dispute:

  • Invoice Matching Agent finds the matching shipment record and flags what doesn’t line up.
  • Pricing Variance Agent compares the carrier’s charge against the contracted rate and determines whether the difference is valid.
  • Accessorial Validation Agent checks whether unexpected fees (such as residential delivery or liftgate charges) are supported by the actual delivery events.

Each agent pulls specific carrier billing rules and policies before making a recommendation. After the exception is resolved, the system generates a plain-language note explaining what was found and what action was taken.

Each custom agent has an instruction prompt (defining its role, decision boundaries, and output format), a set of actions (integrations into SpeedShip), and access to carrier-specific knowledge bases. By using Amazon Bedrock, each agent accesses a suitable foundation model through a single API while inheriting existing AWS governance. For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

Actions

The agents connect to SpeedShip through the same APIs that analysts use. That means the AI sees exactly what a human reviewer would see (contract rates, shipment details, delivery proof) and writes its resolution into the same workflow. SpeedShip has APIs on AWS, so the agents wire into the same endpoints as other existing systems.

Carrier knowledge base

Every carrier has different billing rules, fee definitions, and dispute procedures. Worldwide Express stores each carrier’s documentation: tariff rules, surcharge definitions, dispute steps, and variance thresholds. When an agent processes an exception, it retrieves that specific carrier’s policies and standard operating procedure (SOP) documents before deciding, so each decision is grounded in the carrier’s own rules. The same three agents handle all carriers without any carrier-specific code.

Human-in-the-loop

The approval step was necessary for FinOps adoption during the initial rollout. Initially, a human reviewer would use the existing SpeedShip UI to approve recommendations before they’re finalized. Eventually when accuracy exceeded 99 percent, bulk approval became the default.

Observability

Worldwide Express’s team built dashboards tracking automation rate by carrier, error rate by exception type, resolution time, and human override frequency. When a reviewer rejects a recommendation, the system logs the feedback. The team refines instruction prompts and knowledge bases based on rejection history, steadily increasing automation coverage.

End-to-end flow

The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow, from exception detection through the three specialized agents to human approval. In the diagram, exceptions from the data sources (the SpeedShip TMS, a shipping system, an electronic data interchange (EDI) server, and carrier and vendor portals) are detected and routed to one of three agents. Each agent runs on Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling, uses an agent framework with its own prompt, tools, and carrier knowledge base, and calls Amazon Bedrock for model inference. The agents produce a resolution report. Cost finalization and an AI-written note then go to a human reviewer for approval in the SpeedShip analyst UI.

Results

Six months in, Worldwide Express has deployed the solution across over 40 LTL carriers. The agents currently close 10,000 (approximately 50 percent) exceptions weekly with a less than 1 percent error rate. This shifted the FinOps team’s time from routine resolution to complex, high-value disputes.

The impact shows up most clearly in the backlog of active exceptions, which fell from $15M in June 2025 to $4M six months later, a 75 percent reduction. Worldwide Express unlocked $10M in freed-up cash flow, over $1M in annual cost savings, and 60x first-year ROI. The company reports time-to-cash improving by four weeks.

“With AWS, we’ve automated more than 40 percent of weekly billing exceptions, significantly reducing costs and accelerating billing cycles from days to minutes. Today, we release approximately $10 million more in customer billings each week at a speed that simply wasn’t possible before.”

— Nathanael Pearson, VP of FinOps, Worldwide Express

Looking forward

Worldwide Express is already expanding this approach to other parts of the Order-to-Cash cycle. For logistics companies managing high carrier volumes, the path forward is to start small. Automate the most repetitive exception type first, prove accuracy, then scale across the rest of the portfolio.

Conclusion

Worldwide Express’s exception automation shows what’s possible when agentic AI meets a well-scoped business problem. The combination of Amazon Bedrock, carrier-specific knowledge bases, and a human-in-the-loop approval design let Worldwide Express move from assessment to production in less than 6 months while maintaining financial controls. The company is now expanding automation to other Order-to-Cash processes.

To explore whether a similar approach might work for your organization, request a conversation with your account team or learn more about Amazon Bedrock. Partners like LTM can run a Proof of Value sprint with your own data.

entries.title: Configure the ChatGPT desktop app with Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)
entries.summary: The ChatGPT desktop app is now available on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US). This post walks through a controlled local deployment that routes model inference to Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US-West) using API-mode sign-in, a managed device policy, a named AWS profile, and network restrictions, so a security team can validate it before broader use.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Configure the ChatGPT desktop app with Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)

The ChatGPT desktop app is now available on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US), providing access to OpenAI’s frontier models through two components. Work completes complex, multi-step tasks and delivers review-ready results, and Codex is a coding agent for developing, testing, and reviewing software.

This walkthrough is intended for organizations whose security architecture requires model inference to use AWS GovCloud (US) identities, endpoints, and Regional controls. It configures Codex to route model requests through Amazon Bedrock Mantle in 

us-gov-west-1
, where access can be governed using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and existing AWS GovCloud (US) network controls.

Codex is the OpenAI coding agent for AI-powered software development. With GPT models powering inference, Codex introduces a new class of intelligence optimized for complex, long-horizon developer workflows. You can use the ChatGPT desktop app, the Codex CLI, and IDE integrations with Visual Studio Code, JetBrains, and Xcode. Model inference is routed through the Responses API on Amazon Bedrock.

For customers with data residency requirements, processing stays within the Amazon Bedrock AWS Region that you select. You pay per token with no seat licenses and no per-developer commitments. Zero data retention (ZDR) is also supported. In this configurable mode, prompts and responses are processed without being written to durable storage by AWS or shared with model providers. This helps you protect sensitive information and meet stringent data-governance, privacy, and security requirements.

This post walks through a controlled local deployment of the ChatGPT desktop app that sends model inference to Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US-West). The configuration uses API-mode sign-in, a managed device policy, a named AWS profile, and network restrictions. These restrictions allow access only to the approved Amazon Bedrock endpoint while disabling other external connections and network-enabled capabilities. The result is a deployment that an agency security team can test and document before approving broader use.

Using AWS GovCloud (US) and following this guide do not, by themselves, authorize your workload. Your organization remains responsible for reviewing the selected model, AWS services, Region, endpoint, workstation controls, repositories, credentials, and data flows against its system security plan and authorization process.

Solution overview

You can use the ChatGPT desktop app in two ways:

  • Work for larger tasks that need planning, research, files, and a finished result.
  • Codex for technical work such as editing code, running tests, and reviewing pull requests.

The ChatGPT desktop app runs on an organization-managed computer through the desktop app or CLI. It uses the configured AWS credentials to securely send requests to the Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoint in 

us-gov-west-1
. Because this setup uses AWS directly, ChatGPT workspace rules and user roles don’t control it. The main security controls are the computer’s policies and the AWS identity and permissions being used.

Walkthrough

The configuration has three main steps: set up authentication, set up the ChatGPT desktop app configuration files, and then launch, initialize, and verify the deployment.

Prerequisites

Before setting up the ChatGPT desktop app with AWS GovCloud (US), make sure your version of the ChatGPT desktop app supports Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US). You need an approved AWS GovCloud (US) account, an IAM identity and approved credentials, access to the approved model, AWS Region, and endpoint, and permission to use them. You also need to set up the 

requirements.toml
and 
config.toml
files.

Step 1: Set up authentication

Select the approved AWS GovCloud (US) account and IAM identity or role with access to the approved model in 

us-gov-west-1
. Obtain credentials through your organization’s approved mechanism. This walkthrough uses the named profile 
codex-il5
. Keep credentials, bearer tokens, session tokens, and other secrets out of TOML files.

Protect the profile configuration, credential source, SSO token cache, and any credential helper from ChatGPT desktop app task writes, while allowing approved authentication tools to maintain and refresh credentials.

The ChatGPT desktop app supports two Amazon Bedrock authentication pathways: an Amazon Bedrock API key or the AWS SDK credential chain. AWS SSO through AWS IAM Identity Center is supported within the credential-chain pathway.

The app first checks for 

AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK
in its environment. For desktop use, this variable can be supplied through 
%USERPROFILE%\.codex\.env
on Windows or 
~/.codex/.env
on Linux and macOS. When present, the bearer token takes precedence over profile-based authentication.

If no bearer token is available, the app falls back to the standard AWS SDK credential chain. The chain can read AWS credentials from 

~/.aws/credentials
and related profile settings from 
~/.aws/config
. On Windows, the corresponding default paths are 
%USERPROFILE%\.aws\credentials
and 
%USERPROFILE%\.aws\config
. The chain also supports SSO profiles. For SSO, it uses the profile settings in the AWS config file and the cached SSO session to obtain temporary role credentials. These credentials don’t need to be manually stored in the AWS credentials file. See OpenAI’s Bedrock authentication documentation and the AWS IAM Identity Center credential provider documentation.

Step 2: Set up ChatGPT desktop app configuration files

You must create two ChatGPT desktop app configuration files: 

config.toml
and 
requirements.toml
.

Important: the configuration files need to be set up before the application is launched. The following table shows the file locations.

Operating systemUser

Start from the 

requirements.toml
file. 
requirements.toml
is an administrator-controlled rules file. It sets security limits that users can’t override, for example, restricting which permission levels, tools, or settings the ChatGPT desktop app is allowed to use.

Use the following baseline for the supported AWS GovCloud (US) Amazon Bedrock deployment. The 

[windows]
section applies only to Windows, and 
sandbox_private_desktop
must be supported by the approved runtime.

Next, configure the 

config.toml
file. 
config.toml
tells the ChatGPT desktop app how to operate, including which model provider to use (
amazon-bedrock
), which model to select, and settings such as permissions or context limits.

Replace the model ID and named profile (for example, 

codex-il5
) with approved values.

Step 3: Launch, initialize, and verify

Download the app from the ChatGPT site and install it. Leave the app closed after installation. If it opens automatically or if the app has been launched previously, fully exit ChatGPT and end any lingering ChatGPT or Codex processes.

Make sure 

requirements.toml
and 
config.toml
are in place before the first app launch.

Start the app to load the 

requirements.toml

config.toml
settings. Make sure it shows 
amazon-bedrock
as the model provider.

In the Codex CLI, you should see a 

/status
tab that looks like this:

In the ChatGPT desktop app, you can also confirm 

amazon-bedrock
as the model provider.

Troubleshooting

The application prompts for an OpenAI account. Verify that 

requirements.toml
and 
config.toml
use the exact locations and file names shown in the preceding table, terminate all ChatGPT and Codex processes, and relaunch. The files must precede app launch.

AWS GovCloud (US) endpoint is reported as unsupported. Confirm the exact desktop or app-server release, endpoint, and model with OpenAI. Changing the URL alone does not establish support.

The wrong AWS identity is used. Inspect the effective credential source and named profile. Check whether an Amazon Bedrock API key takes precedence over the profile.

Capability restrictions are missing. Inspect the full effective requirements after restart. The API-only sign-in setting doesn’t apply the capability policy.

Rollback and cleanup

If a validation check fails, stop the rollout. Return the affected devices to the previously approved policy and provider settings, then restart the ChatGPT desktop app. Revoke any temporary AWS credentials or API keys, and confirm that those devices can no longer connect to Amazon Bedrock. Keep a record of the test and clearly document what failed before trying again.

Conclusion

The ChatGPT desktop app on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US) gives you a controlled way to use OpenAI frontier models and coding assistance. Inference stays in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. By validating the configuration, confirming the approved AWS identity and endpoint, and verifying security controls, you can confidently prepare the deployment for broader use. This approach supports innovation while aligning deployment decisions with each organization’s security, authorization, and data-handling requirements.

Ready to explore the ChatGPT desktop app with Codex on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)? Start with a controlled deployment, validate your security controls, and work with your security team to prepare for broader adoption.

  • Responses API on Amazon Bedrock – AWS Regions, endpoint behavior, authentication, and permissions for the Responses API.
  • AWS GovCloud (US) compliance – Compliance programs and customer authorization considerations.
  • OpenAI’s Bedrock authentication documentation – Amazon Bedrock API key and AWS SDK credential-chain authentication, including SSO.

entries.title: How the UK Amazon Quick User Group grew in 2026
entries.summary: The UK Amazon Quick User Group's 2026 roundup: three quarterly meetups, 150+ attendees, and customer stories from Arriva, Carsa, and Propulse Lab on using agentic AI and Amazon Quick to turn data into faster decisions, higher satisfaction, and scalable growth.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How the UK Amazon Quick User Group grew in 2026

The Amazon Quick User Group – United Kingdom is a community of Amazon Quick users in the United Kingdom who meet quarterly to exchange knowledge, share best practices, learn through hands-on sessions, and discuss their experiences using the service. These user groups function as collaborative forums where members learn, connect, and innovate together.

Whether you’re already using Amazon Quick or just getting started, we’d love for you to join the UK Amazon Quick User Group and become part of a growing community that’s redefining how organizations make decisions with data. In this post, we’re thrilled to share our 2026 yearly roundup, highlighting all three quarterly meetups that have taken place since the group’s launch and the momentum that has followed. The events drew more than 150 attendees, and the energy in the room, fueled by agentic AI and the potential of Amazon Quick, was clear. Across industries, customers are using Amazon Quick to turn data chaos into faster decisions, higher satisfaction, and scalable growth. Their work spans real-time incident management, eliminating dashboard sprawl with governed data layers, and automating most support workflows with AI.

Why Amazon Quick user groups matter

The UK Amazon Quick User Group is a local community of Amazon Quick users who come together quarterly to share knowledge, best practices, and experiences with the service. Amazon Quick user groups serve as collaborative forums where members can:

  • Learn and share – Exchange real-world insights about the capabilities of Amazon Quick, from interactive dashboards and data storytelling to agentic AI-powered automations and custom agents. Members share what works, what doesn’t, and new approaches that drive results.
  • Network – Connect with regional professionals who are solving similar use cases with Amazon Quick for enterprise AI applications, data analytics, and workplace productivity.
  • Problem-solve – Tackle challenges collaboratively by discussing solutions and use cases across different industries and business contexts.
  • Stay updated – Get firsthand knowledge about new features, updates, and emerging best practices directly from peers and experts.
  • Build community – Foster a local support network that complements the broader Amazon Quick community, with trusted contacts who understand UK market and business context.

Event overview

Over three quarterly meetups this year, the UK community spent real time with Amazon Quick. Not slide decks about it, actual time building with it. People created Amazon Quick custom chat agents for their teams without writing code. They tried Amazon Quick Desktop running on their own laptops, connected to local files and using a connector to access Outlook. They also used Amazon Quick Apps to turn a plain-language description into a working web application. The workshops had attendees automating processes with Amazon Quick Flows and Amazon Quick Automate, while Amazon Quick Research showed how it significantly cuts down the time spent on research. The Amazon Quick chat agent tied it together, an assistant that connects to tools, data and takes actions on your behalf. Every quarter, the sessions got more practical and the questions from the room got sharper.

What a typical event looks like

All three events were held at the Amazon UK Corporate Office in Shoreditch, London. By 9:45 AM, the room is already buzzing. People reconnect over coffee, swap updates from the last quarter, and newcomers get pulled into conversations before the day even officially begins.

From there, the energy carries through the full agenda: customers share real stories about what they’ve built with Amazon Quick, product leads walk through the latest updates, and panels spark the kind of back-and-forth you don’t get from a webinar. The 75-minute hands-on workshop is where it really comes alive, with attendees rolling up their sleeves in provisioned sandbox accounts and experimenting together. By the time we close with a feedback session, the room feels more like a working group than an audience.

The format has shifted each quarter. Q1 leaned more on introductions and demos because the group was meeting for the first time. By Q2, we added an icebreaker quiz, and ran a focused workshop on Quick Flows and automation. For Q3 we brought in a specialist panel, a group quiz, and a networking slot at the end. That last one came about because people were already staying behind to talk after the close, so we stopped packing up around them and put it in the schedule.

What customers shared

Customer stories have been part of the community from the start. Each speaker brought a different problem into the room, showing how teams are applying Quick in very different environments.

At the first event, the conversation centered on getting insight into the hands of the people who need it. At Arriva UK Trains, critical data wasn’t reaching the people who needed it most. Train and station managers were constantly on the move, relying solely on their work mobiles. Sofia Bourika’s team built dynamic, role-based dashboards with mobile-friendly views and introduced pixel perfect reports automatically delivered through scheduled email, giving managers immediate visibility of incidents and performance. The result: faster decisions, better incident management, and a stronger data-driven culture across the organization.

By Q2, the discussion had moved toward a different challenge: getting the foundations right before introducing more AI and automation. At Carsa, a used-car retailer, analytics functioned like a service desk. Question in, dashboard out. The same question gave different answers. It wasn’t a data problem. It was a definitions problem. Tobi Daramola’s team at Carsa fixed this by building a single governed data layer, with metrics defined once and consumed by Amazon Quick and AI assistants alike. As a result, they removed 50 percent of dashboards while surfacing more data. Customer satisfaction (CSAT) scores moved 10 percent in 30 days, complaints same-day close rate jumped 20 percent, and AI on the layer cut recurring tasks from 45 minutes to 5.

Q3 brought the conversation further into automation and agentic workflows. Propulse Lab, a Swiss operating system for B2C subscription businesses, was handling 1 million support tickets a year. Their teams were stuck firefighting instead of driving growth. After deploying a multi-agent AI pipeline in Amazon Quick Automate, built from their best past customer service interactions, they cut request handling from 7 minutes to 70 seconds. The pipeline also automated 80 percent of routine workflows.

“What was once a cost centre became a growth engine – their product managers now own the entire system without writing a single line of code, and their support teams focus on proactive, revenue-driving conversations instead.”

— Guirec Lecointre, Growth Operations Specialist, Propulse Lab

The use cases vary widely, and that’s exactly the point. Rather than presenting a single vision for Amazon Quick, practitioners show what they’ve tried against real business problems, from governed analytics and frontline reporting to automation and AI. That shifts the conversation in the room. Attendees ask direct questions about implementation, adoption, and what didn’t work. Speakers share the practical lessons behind the finished solution. People leave with ideas they can apply to their own organizations, not just another customer story.

From presentations to participation

Attendees changed across the three events. A listen-and-learn turned into building meaningful relationships by Q3. People were new to the group and new to each other. By Q2, the icebreaker quiz loosened things up early. The feedback sessions got more specific too: instead of “this was great,” people were requesting topics and offering to contribute.

Q3 pushes this further. Sofia Bourika, who joined the leadership team early on and presented the Arriva customer story at the first event, came up with an icebreaker called “What Are You Proud Of?”, attendees share something they’ve built with Amazon Quick. We’ve already got someone who was previously sitting in the audience volunteering to present their work. That kind of shift, from attending to contributing, took three events to happen, but it happened. Q3 also introduced a new segment, the Amazon Quick specialist panel. Questions were pre-collected from the audience and posed to an invited specialist, who brought real depth to the answers and shared first-hand experience of working with attendees’ customers. It sparked a different kind of thinking in the room, with the audience connecting the dots between the specialist’s insights and their own day-to-day challenges.

Our community stayed connected all year. Our LinkedIn group had weekly contributions and our email lists encouraged involvement.

Collective impact in action

A huge thank you to our dedicated AWS Partner, Data Reply, whose consistent contributions and thought leadership have been instrumental in making every UK user group meetup a success.

Our UK leadership team led us to reach every milestone:

Liam Yusuph, AI and Data Delivery Lead, Data Reply

Priyanka Bettaswamygowda, Solutions Architect, AWS

Sahar Shahbaz, Data Analyst, Data Reply

Sofia Bourika, Lead BI Developer, Arriva

Tobi Daramola, Senior Data and Analytics Lead, Carsa

Ali Hayat, AV Support Associate, Amazon

Lam Phan, BI Developer, AWS

Rikhi Singh, ADC Engineer, AWS

Amazon Quick Community resources

The Amazon Quick Community website has tens of thousands of members and thousands of searchable questions. It also offers over 600 learning resources on accelerating your productivity with agentic AI and Amazon Quick.

“The Quick Community is about learning together and building connections. It’s where users at any skill level can find help, learn something new, and meet others. What I love most about the Quick Community is how genuinely helpful everyone is. It’s a place that reveals possibilities you wouldn’t have thought to explore on your own, where you stumble into people working on projects and use cases, you’d never even think to ask about, and suddenly your world gets a whole lot bigger.”

— Kristin Mandia, Sr. Community Manager, AWS

Learning opportunities include approximately two free live online sessions per week, monthly feature update detailed and advanced automation sessions, and 4-hour Immersion Day workshops. AWS Solutions Architects, Product Managers, and subject matter experts are active on the platform and available for direct messaging. Kristin continues, “People jump in to help solve tricky problems, share their clever workarounds, and experiment with new ways to use Quick together.”

Key takeaways

A few themes came up consistently across the three events.

The format keeps changing because we listen

The Amazon Quick User Group UK runs on a set structure: an introduction, a product update, customer stories, a hands-on workshop, and a feedback session. But we’ve been adjusting it every quarter. Early on, we had the “What’s New with Quick” segment right after customer stories, and it broke the flow. People were engaged with how a real company was using the product, then we’d switch to feature announcements. We moved “What’s New” so the customer stories lead straight into the workshop, and the difference was noticeable. For Q3, we added an interactive quiz to get more back-and-forth going in the room. Attendees also called out the overall format and pacing, and the chance to meet new people. As one first-time attendee put it, “the networking opportunities were excellent… I thoroughly enjoyed the day!”.

Customers present, not us

At least one customer shares how they use Amazon Quick at each event. Across three events, we’ve had Carsa, Arriva, Propulse Lab, and a few other customers on stage. After the very first event, one of the clearest pieces of feedback was that people wanted more customer speakers. That told us we were on the right track. The sessions work because the audience is hearing from peers who face similar problems, not from someone trying to sell them something. The impact goes beyond the event itself. Attendees said the customer stories showed them new ways to use the tools and started useful discussions about return on investment (ROI). One attendee told us a customer session “has already prompted a lot of conversation internally” at their organization.

The workshop is where it clicks

Every event has a hands-on workshop, and people consistently tell us it’s the part they get the most out of. There’s a gap between watching someone demo a product and sitting down with it yourself. That gap is where most attendees say Amazon Quick starts to make sense for what they’re trying to do. We know it lands because the most common question afterwards is whether they can keep access to the workshop environment so they can carry on experimenting on their own.

Conclusion
